originalObjects.reason: All three kinetic-theory ideas and their experimental basis survive. Continuous irregular motion is stated inside an ordinary-condition classical model, not as a universal microscopic trajectory law. The added limit qualifies the source's overbroad wording without substituting a new topic.

The paraffin/iron example, internal-structure comparison and two-way connection between thermal phenomena and particle models are preserved. Iron warming/expansion is not denied and no iron phase change at the paraffin temperature is asserted.

Upper-atmosphere gas, terrestrial solids, planetary cores and stellar cores all remain. The source's alternatives of molecules, atoms and smaller charged particles remain alternatives dependent on conditions, not a claim that every example is molecular or classically described.

originalObjects.label: footnote
originalObjects.reason: The atom/molecule footnote stays with N4 and retains its marker and object identity. Chemical identity is distinguished from bulk properties; the molecule definition is explicitly restricted to molecular substances rather than being imposed on ionic and metallic solids.

paragraphReviews.textAndReadability: A compact parallel three-item introduction clearly names particles, microscopic thermal motion and mutual interaction. The next paragraph explains the motion instead of leaving the source's absolute claim unqualified.
paragraphReviews.scienceAndFidelity: Preserves the source's three ideas without turning 'matter consists of particles' into 'all matter consists of molecules'. The classical scope in paragraphs 1-2 applies to the motion statement.

paragraphReviews.textAndReadability: Two short sentences attach 'ongoing and irregular' directly to the thermal motion just introduced. The evidence statement is qualified without a claim of proof at every possible temperature or density.
paragraphReviews.scienceAndFidelity: The continuous irregular-motion idea and experimental support remain, but the ordinary-condition classical model is expressly bounded. This is independently assessed as appropriate; no historical science approval is invoked.

paragraphReviews.textAndReadability: The single sentence closes the introductory model group before the heating example. It states what the model does not imply, without requiring a new quantum-mechanics lesson.
paragraphReviews.scienceAndFidelity: Rejects universal classical random trajectories. Very cold and extremely dense matter are relevant examples of classical-model limits; the wording does not claim that only these conditions can require a different description.

paragraphReviews.textAndReadability: Three sentences move from thermal processes to the source's concrete comparison. 'The same temperature' supplies an understandable common endpoint for paraffin and iron.
paragraphReviews.scienceAndFidelity: 'A few tens of degrees Celsius can melt it' preserves the qualitative source temperature without inventing one exact melting point for all paraffin mixtures. Iron remains solid at that temperature but warms and can expand. Neither 'iron does not change' nor 'iron melts too' is stated.

paragraphReviews.textAndReadability: The explanation follows the example, then closes with the source's two-way relationship: observations inform a structure model, and the model explains thermal phenomena.
paragraphReviews.scienceAndFidelity: Internal structures and interactions account for the contrasting thermal responses. The wording does not suggest that heat can be understood from an unchanged structure alone or discard the original explanatory purpose.

paragraphReviews.textAndReadability: The broad survey comes after the local material example. Three sentences separate the locations, explanatory factors and condition-dependent particle types.
paragraphReviews.scienceAndFidelity: All four source settings are retained. Properties depend on particles, motion and interactions; the text does not claim these settings share one molecular constitution or that stellar cores contain intact molecules. The atom footnote callout remains attached to atoms.

paragraphReviews.textAndReadability: A direct first sentence prevents the preceding examples being read as an all-matter-molecular claim. The second provides the needed extreme-condition qualification without introducing a new apparatus, calculation or exercise.
paragraphReviews.scienceAndFidelity: Atoms/molecules may lose integrity at extreme temperatures or densities, and a simple classical molecular model may be inadequate. 'May' appropriately avoids claiming universal ionization or dissociation for every extreme material.

paragraphReviews.textAndReadability: The footnote first defines an atom, then explicitly scopes the molecule description, then distinguishes one molecule from a whole sample. The technical vocabulary is formal but the three sentences keep the distinctions separate.
paragraphReviews.scienceAndFidelity: An atom is described as the smallest unit retaining an element's chemical identity, not all its bulk properties. A molecular substance's molecule is a discrete neutral bonded group of atoms. 'Molecular identity' is chemically scoped; the following sentence expressly rejects assigning every macroscopic bulk property to one molecule.

paragraphReviews.textAndReadability: The short closing qualification remains within the footnote's concept group rather than being separated as a new topic.
paragraphReviews.scienceAndFidelity: Ordinary ionic and metallic solids are not defined as collections of separate molecules. This prevents the original generic molecule definition from being overextended and does not erase the source's atom/molecule distinction.

identityAndMath.reason: N4 has no source equations or math tokens to alter. Lesson number 4, physical start page 16, printed start page 7 and per-object printed pages 7/8 remain exact. 'A few tens' stays qualitative, with no invented precise melting temperature. Math and figure 2 in the neighboring N5 material on page 0017 are outside N4 and have not been imported.
